title: Italy Signs $4.2B DDX Destroyer Deal as NATO Shifts Command to Europe and Warns of Russian Maritime Drone Threat
subhead: Italy ordered two 13,500-ton DDX destroyers for €3.7 billion, NATO's SACEUR said the US will provide 'critical but more limited capabilities' as Europeans take a larger role, and a CIA warning surfaced of Russian Gerbera drones launched from Mediterranean merchant vessels.

sections.heading: Italy Signs €3.7B Deal for Two DDX Destroyers
sections.body: Italy signed a €3.7 billion ($4.2 billion) contract for two new DDX destroyers, brokered through European procurement agency OCCAR and awarded to Orizzonte Sistemi Navali (OSN) — a joint venture in which state shipyard Fincantieri holds 51% and state defense group Leonardo the remaining 49%, Defense News reports. The 13,500-tonne, 180-meter vessels will carry a crew of 251, have a 4,000-nautical-mile range, and are slated for delivery in 2033 and 2035. Leonardo's combat system will be built around its SADOC 5 command-and-control suite, a digital S-band AESA radar and MBDA weapon systems, along with a DC power sub-network, integrated energy storage and an innovative stabilization system tied to the steering system. The destroyers will sail alongside but ultimately replace the navy's two Horizon vessels, a navy spokesman told Defense News, extending a fleet renewal splurge that has already covered FREMM frigates, PPA multimission ships, a new landing helicopter dock, submarines and logistics vessels.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal consolidates Italy's state-owned naval industrial base (Fincantieri-Leonardo) into a single prime for future warships and signals Rome's commitment to high-end European surface combatants at a time of heightened Baltic and Mediterranean tensions — a direct counterpoint to the US signaling a smaller role in NATO.

sections.heading: SACEUR: US to Provide 'Critical but More Limited' Capabilities to NATO
sections.body: NATO's top commander, US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, said the United States would continue to provide 'critical but more limited capabilities' to the alliance as Europeans take on a greater role defending the continent, Reuters reports. Speaking en route to a change-of-command ceremony at NATO's Joint Force Command Norfolk, where a British army general is taking over from a US Navy vice admiral, Grynkewich also said NATO was stepping up intelligence-sharing in response to a wave of sabotage and other incidents apparently linked to Russia. He dismissed any notion that Moscow might exploit US stockpile exhaustion after the war with Iran, saying of a limited Russian attack on NATO territory: 'Absolutely not. He better not try it on my watch.' The remarks followed a Danish defense intelligence warning that Russia was likely to intensify hybrid war against the West in coming months and posed 'a low but growing risk' of a limited military attack on a NATO member bordering Russia.
sections.whyItMatters: The Norfolk handover to a European commander marks a concrete step in the Trump-driven burden-shift to Europe — the first structural signal that the US is institutionalizing a reduced NATO posture, even as it retains the alliance's most sensitive high-end capabilities.

sections.heading: Report: CIA Warned Europe of Russian Drone Launches From Mediterranean Vessels
sections.body: The CIA has warned European countries of a suspected Russian plot to launch Gerbera-type drones from commercial vessels in the Mediterranean, according to a report in Spanish daily El Mundo based on an anonymous Lithuanian intelligence source and cited by Defense News. The assessment reportedly named Spain, France or Italy as potential targets, with drones launched from international waters and reaching coastal countries within one to two hours. The Gerbera has a 2.5-meter wingspan, a maximum range of 600 kilometers and a small warhead suited to starting fires or damaging exposed infrastructure, per El Mundo. The drones are said to be concealed in shipping containers and catapult-launched. European governments were reportedly briefed shortly after CIA director's unannounced visit to Moscow on Aug. 25, and the report coincides with French President Emmanuel Macron convening a Defense Council on Sept. 16. Defense News notes the El Mundo report has not been independently corroborated.
sections.whyItMatters: If confirmed, this points to a Russian shift toward covert, deniable maritime drone attacks against NATO rear areas — a threat that combines the shadow fleet's logistics reach with cheap loitering munitions, and one that European navies are only beginning to equip themselves to counter.

sections.heading: Saildrone Logs First National Flag Registration With Denmark
sections.body: US unmanned-surface-vehicle maker Saildrone said the first four Voyager USVs have been registered under the Danish flag — the first time one of its vehicles operates under any national flag, the company told Defense News. The 33-foot Voyager, powered by an electric motor with a mapping speed of 5 knots, can operate for 100 days between service stops, performing continuous maritime ISR, seafloor characterization and real-time domain awareness. Saildrone's European head of business development said the Danish Navy and government are creating a new contract for more units, and the firm is in talks with several European navies while ramping up USV production with partners in the Netherlands, Norway and Poland. The company is also developing Spectre, a 170-foot USV due in 2027 that will be its largest and fastest platform and, uniquely, carry weapons via containerized kinetic payloads.
sections.whyItMatters: Denmark's position guarding the Danish Straits between the Baltic and North Seas makes it a natural early adopter for persistent, low-cost maritime surveillance; the flag registration is a commercial milestone for USV exports and points to a fast-growing European market for uncrewed surface assets that also carries a precedent for the armed Spectre class.

sections.heading: Army Awards Palantir $48.1M to Overhaul Ammunition Management
sections.body: The US Army awarded a Palantir Technologies subsidiary a $48.1 million contract to develop software that consolidates nine separate legacy ammunition platforms into a single lifecycle-tracking system, Defense News reports. The new tool uses 'commercial low-code, no-code technology' and lets soldiers track munitions from 'planning, production, and procurement, to storage, surveillance, distribution, expenditure, and final disposition,' per the service. The award followed a three-phase, six-week selection process. It responds to problems documented in the Army's Line of Departure journal, which found ammunition forecasts at lower levels often rely on assumptions and historical trends rather than actual demand tied to training cycles, with disconnected systems failing to reflect schedule changes in real time. Palantir already contributes to Army Vantage, Next Generation Command and Control, and the Tactical Intelligence Targeting Access Node, and operates the cross-branch Maven Smart System.
sections.whyItMatters: The contract extends Palantir's defense footprint from intelligence and targeting into logistics — a quiet but consequential step as the Army tries to fix audit readiness and ammunition accountability problems that strained supply chains during the Iran conflict and Ukraine's artillery war.

sections.heading: Germany Lobbies US to Manufacture PAC-3 Interceptors
sections.body: German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has lobbied US defense leaders to allow production of PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles in Germany, arguing an additional site would ease a global shortfall in air-defense weapons, Defense News reports. The push builds on last week's US-German agreement to expand shared Patriot production signed with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon. Pistorius said Berlin wants to manufacture all elements of the Patriot value chain — PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors and launchers — plus other American weaponry in short supply among allies. Germany's MBDA already builds PAC-2 interceptors (a Raytheon product), while the more advanced PAC-3 MSE is made by Lockheed Martin, which has a long-standing cooperation agreement with Rheinmetall. Whether German or European production proceeds is largely up to the US government and Lockheed, given the performance characteristics of Patriot interceptors are closely guarded — and the weapons have been a decades-old revenue source for both Boeing's successor manufacturers and Washington.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a test case for how far the US will go in sharing licensed production of its most sensitive air-defense technology — a tension between allied demand, the 'cash cow' economics of Patriot, and the security concerns around exporting interceptors that Ukraine was similarly promised under license earlier this year.

sections.heading: South Korea Faces Dilemma Over Trump's Iran Mission Troop Requests
sections.body: South Korea is weighing US requests to contribute forces to Washington's Iran campaign, a decision that experts warn could leave Seoul exposed when it matters most in its own theater, Defense News reports. The story notes that contributing troops to a distant American war carries reputational and deterrence costs, while refusing could strain the alliance at a moment when Seoul depends on US extended deterrence against North Korea. It follows broader allied pressure on the Trump administration's Iran mission, which has already drawn reluctant participation from other partners and renewed debate over burden-sharing. Defense News framed the choice as one with 'no good options' for Seoul.
sections.whyItMatters: Seoul's decision is a barometer for how US allies in the Asia-Pacific respond to being pulled into Washington's Middle East campaigns — and whether the Trump-era demand that allies bear more of the cost of their own security will translate into their joining conflicts far from home.

bottomLine: Today's defense picture is defined by a rebalancing of the Western alliance around a less expansive US role: NATO formally handed its Norfolk command to a European officer even as SACEUR Grynkewich framed American support as 'critical but more limited,' Italy signed a €3.7 billion state-owned destroyer order, and Europe grappled with an unverified but alarming CIA warning of Russian Gerbera drones being launched from Mediterranean merchant ships. On the industry side, Palantir deepened its logistics footprint, Germany pressed Washington to license PAC-3 production, and Saildrone logged its first national-flag USV registration with Denmark — while South Korea weighed the political cost of contributing to America's Iran mission. The through-line is a shift from US-led reassurance toward allied self-sufficiency and a more contested, hybrid-threat environment that is reshaping both procurement priorities and industrial strategy across Europe and Asia.
sources: Defense News (Italy DDX deal; NATO SACEUR via Reuters; CIA Mediterranean drone warning via El Mundo; Saildrone Denmark; Palantir ammo contract; Germany PAC-3; South Korea Iran mission)
